'''Peter J. Rossky''' is an American theoretical chemist who has worked on understanding molecular processes in condensed phases. He serves as the Harry C. & Olga K. Wiess Chair in Natural Sciences and Professor of Chemistry at [[Rice University]].

Rossky is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-04-17 |title=Peter Rossky is 2018-19 Hirschfelder Prize Recipient |url=https://chem.wisc.edu/2018/04/17/peter-rossky-is-2018-19-hirschfelder-prize-recipient/?utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=2025-04-01 |website=Department of Chemistry |language=en-US}}</ref>{{AI-retrieved source|date=April 2026}}

== Education and career ==
Rossky earned his undergraduate degree in Chemistry [[Latin honors|summa cum laude]] from [[Cornell University]]. He completed his Ph.D. in Chemical Physics at [[Harvard University]] in 1978 under the mentorship of [[Martin Karplus]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rossky |first=Peter J. |date=2020-11-25 |title=An Autobiographical History of Peter J. Rossky |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c09811 |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |volume=124 |issue=47 |pages=10594–10597 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c09811 |issn=1520-6106|doi-access=free }}</ref>  Following a postdoctoral fellowship at [[Stony Brook University|SUNY Stony Brook]] with Harold Friedman, he joined the faculty at the [[University of Texas at Austin|University of Texas]] at [[Austin, Texas|Austin]] in 1979.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}} There, he held the Marvin K. Collie-Welch Regents Chair in Chemistry and served as Director of the Center for Computational Molecular Sciences. In 2014, Rossky joined [[Rice University]] as the Dean of the [[Wiess School of Natural Sciences]], a position he held until 2021, after which he continued as a professor and researcher.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Falk |first=Jeff |title=Thomas Killian named dean of Wiess School of Natural Sciences |url=https://news.rice.edu/news/2020/thomas-killian-named-dean-wiess-school-natural-sciences |website=Rice University News and Media Relations}}</ref>

== Research ==
Rossky contributed to understanding molecular processes in condensed phase systems. He worked on theoretical and computational studies of chemical and biomolecular structures, reaction dynamics, and electronic processes within liquid environments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pettitt |first=B. Montgomery |last2=Schwartz |first2=Benjamin J. |last3=Sterpone |first3=Fabio |last4=Túri |first4=László |last5=Willard |first5=Adam P. |date=2020-11-25 |title=Tribute to Peter J. Rossky |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c09810 |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B |volume=124 |issue=47 |pages=10591–10593 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpcb.0c09810 |issn=1520-6106|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A central theme in Rossky's work is elucidating the role of liquids, particularly water, as active participants in chemical reactions. Utilizing [[molecular dynamics]] simulations, he has explored the structure and behavior of liquid water at various interfaces, including hydrophobic interactions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter J. Rossky |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=xFQVNpYAAAAJ&utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=2025-04-01 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>{{AI-retrieved source|date=April 2026}} Rossky has also investigated the influence of water on electron-initiated processes and radical chemistry, addressing complex issues in this domain.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}

An additional area of his research focuses on the quantum mechanical behavior of molecular systems in condensed phases. He has developed methods to evaluate spectroscopic signatures of molecular species and track the evolution of energy in electronically excited states. His has worked on the hydrated electron, through quantum simulations of its structure, spectroscopy, and dynamics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Peter J. Rossky |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/peter-j-rossky-8hqd1n/?utm_source=chatgpt.com |access-date=2025-04-01 |website=National Academy of Sciences |language=en-US}}</ref>{{AI-retrieved source|date=April 2026}}
